highlights.text: On his dark gray shoulder-cloak was a silver brooch: a bridge of stone, lit by ruby flames. A Bridgeburner.
“The First Sword of Empire. Dassem Ultor. We heard in the capital before we left. He’s dead. Is it true? Is Dassem dead?”
“You’re with the Third. I thought the Third was with him, in Seven Cities. At Y’ghatan—” “Hood’s Breath, they’re still looking for his body in the still-hot rubble of that damned city,
“Every decision you make can change the world. The best life is the one the gods don’t notice. You want to live free, boy, live quietly.”
Taking up the sword is the last act of desperate men. Mark my words and find yourself a more worthy dream.”
“Do you walk away from this?” the sergeant asked. Tattersail smiled. “The only death I fear is dying ignorant.
“We’ve got to get going,” Fiddler grated. “There’s a knife out there, and it’s got blood on it.”
High House Shadow, and a knife in the dark. A new game’s begun, or the old one’s just turned.
“Play on, mortal. Every god falls at a mortal’s hands. Such is the only end to immortality.”
“It will be a fine day for a walk, pronounces Kruppe, who is wise in all things.”

“There are worms within your empire’s flesh. But such degradation is natural in all bodies. Your people’s infection is not yet fatal. It can be scoured clean. The Moranth are skilled at such efforts.”
“Should you ever outrun the guilt within your past, Sorceress, you will have outrun your soul. When it finds you again it will kill you.”

“Tell me, Tool, what dominates your thoughts?” The Imass shrugged before replying. “I think of futility, Adjunct.” “Do all Imass think about futility?” “No. Few think at all.” “Why is that?” The Imass leaned his head to one side and regarded her. “Because, Adjunct, it is futile.”
Betrayal was the greatest of all crimes in Rallick’s mind, for it took all that was human within a person and made it a thing of pain.

“I know why we fear this Jaghut Tyrant. Because he became human, he became like us, he enslaved, he destroyed, and he did it better than we could.” She lowered her head into her hands. “That’s why we fear.”
Through the gamut of life we struggled for control, for a means to fashion the world around us, an eternal, hopeless hunt for the privilege of being able to predict the shape of our lives.
“It is easy to fool oneself,” Rake answered, “into viewing those beneath one as small and insignificant. The risks of oversight, you might say.”
But, lo, is Kruppe deceived? Can an eel swim? Hurrah, these seeming muddy waters are home to Kruppe, and his eyes are wide with wonder!”
“There are times, Kruppe murmurs, when celibacy born of sad deprivation becomes a boon, nay, a source of great relief. Dear Murillio, prepare for a storm.”

I’ve done my part. Just another nameless stranger who couldn’t run from the face of tyranny. Dear Hood, take the man’s shriveled soul—his dreams are over, ended by an assassin’s whim. As for my own soul, well, you shall have to wait a while longer.
“Then the story begins, as always, with Kruppe . . .” Murillio groaned. “Thus spake the Eel.”
